bib.title: Continuity Errors (Chapter 7 of Statistics Done Wrong)

read.skipped: Chapter footnotes 1-4 are not in the PDF text; year not printed in the excerpt.

question: What goes wrong when continuous variables are split into groups before analysis, and what should be done instead?

results.claim: Choosing the cutoff that gives the smallest p value inflates the false positive rate by up to a factor of 10.
results.source: chapter footnote 1 (citation not printed in the extracted text)
results.setup: Searching over cutoffs to dichotomize a continuous variable and compare the two groups.
results.quote: rate increased by as much as a factor of 10.1
results.note: Footnote marker 1 is fused to the number in the text.

results.claim: Breast cancer S-phase fraction studies that chose the optimal cutoff were significant, but none were after correcting for multiple comparisons.
results.source: early 1990s breast cancer S-phase fraction literature, not named
results.setup: Each study used the median or the best-p-value cutoff between large and small S-phase fractions.
results.quote: But when these were corrected to account for the multiple comparisons, not one of them was statistically signiﬁcant.

results.claim: Dichotomizing loses about as much power and precision as throwing away a third of the data.
results.source: chapter footnote 3 (citation not printed in the extracted text)
results.setup: General statement for splitting a continuous variable into two groups.
results.quote: the same you’d get by throwing away a third of your data.3
results.note: No numeric digit in the value; the claim is the quote.

results.claim: When two correlated predictors are both dichotomized at the median, ANOVA reports a spurious effect of the irrelevant one at a rate set by the test's power, not at the nominal 5%.
results.setup: Wealth and yacht length predicting health-care quality, each split at the median, two-way ANOVA; regression on the continuous variables keeps false positives at the expected rate.
results.quote: this false correlation isn’t statistically signiﬁcant only 5% of the time

limits: No data or simulation of its own; the quantitative claims rest on uncited footnotes (not in the extracted text).
The chapter concedes that strongly correlated predictors are hard to separate even in regression.
practices: Do not arbitrarily split continuous variables into groups; use a procedure that takes full advantage of the continuous variables (Tips, p. 78).
If a split is needed, fix it in advance, reuse the split from similar prior research, or use an outside standard such as a medical definition (Tips, p. 78).
Never choose the cutoff that maximizes significance (p. 74, Tips).
Prefer regression over dichotomized ANOVA when controlling for confounders (pp. 76-77).

terms.definition: It estimates the marginal effect of each variable—the health impact of each additional pound of weight, not just the difference between groups on either side of an arbitrary cutoff.
